summary: The article describes how adult recreational sports leagues, the "Weekend Warriors," are adopting sustainability practices on and off the field. Teams, facilities, consultants and sponsors are cutting single-use plastics, going digital, composting, carpooling and holding educational workshops. Transportation emissions and sustained waste management standards remain the main challenges.
one_line: Adult recreational sports leagues are embracing sustainability through reduced plastics, recycling, digital tools, green facilities and education, though transportation emissions remain a challenge.
key_facts: The article covers the weekend of Saturday, September 2nd, 2023 through Sunday, September 3rd, 2023, when adult athletes fill local sports fields and recreation centers.
Alexandra Torres, captain of the 'Green Goalies' soccer team, said "just showing up and playing wasn't enough" and that teams must take responsibility for the spaces they use.
Michael Johnson, facilities manager at the local recreation center, reports a 40% reduction in single-use plastics since the center began encouraging teams to go green.
Leagues are introducing recycling programs, using digital platforms for scheduling to cut paper use, and coordinating carpooling to reduce travel emissions.
Anita Singh of the 'Basket Ballers' basketball league said her team switched to compostable plates and utensils for after-game socials and encourages players to bring their Tupperware.
Thomas Park's volleyball team, the 'Sand Savers,' has adopted a stretch of the local beach and organizes regular clean-ups and education about plastic pollution.
Rebecca Diaz, a sustainability consultant, connects teams with eco-friendly suppliers and negotiates with facilities to install water refilling stations or solar panels.
Diaz's efforts led a major sporting goods company to donate sustainably-produced uniforms to several local leagues.
Jose Martinez, a software developer and weekend hockey player, urged his team to use public transit or cycle to games after attending a workshop on ocean pollution.
The newly renovated Lincoln Park Sports Complex has a solar-paneled roof and a rainwater harvesting system.
Emily Rios, the Lincoln Park complex's sustainability coordinator, said players feel they are "contributing to something larger than the game."
Transportation to and from events remains a major source of carbon emissions, despite growth in carpooling and public transport use.
Online systems for registration and scheduling, plus apps that track and challenge teams to meet sustainability targets, are reducing paper use and physical meetings.
